transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-29
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Ari Kaplan (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (FluxWare CTO), Emily Torres (ML Eng), Ben Hsu (SRE), Lina Park (Product)

Summary: Quick intake and Optimize console walkthrough focusing on quantization profiles. Customer is latency-sensitive (homepage summarization stream) and cost-aware; interested in an automated playbook for safe rollouts.

[00:00] Ari Kaplan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to walk through our new Speedline quantization playbook inside Optimize and talk through what FP8 and INT8 would mean for your service. Samira's going to run the console and show examples.
[00:22] Rajiv Menon: Thanks Ari, excited to understand tradeoffs. We have a pretty tight 100ms P95 for a lot of user-facing stuff, and we target about 70 to 90ms ideally. Happy to hear what realistically will move the needle.
[00:37] Samira Patel: Great. Couple notes first — when we say Speedline it's our internal playbook name for a conservative-to-aggressive timeline for quant profiles, basically starting with fp16 baseline then introducing INT8 or FP8 depending on sensitivity. It'll show you console recommendations per-route, suggestion of batch sizes, and fallback rules.
[00:56] Emily Torres: Quick Q — can you do mixed precision per route? like low-latency route INT8 and higher-fidelity route FP8?
[01:07] Samira: Yes, that's one of the core things we demo. You can pin a profile per model route, and the runtime supports auto-fallback to a higher-precision variant if quality checks fail. There's also an adaptive mode where we can switch profiles based on load.
[01:28] Ben Hsu: How invasive is it from infra side? We're running FluxWare in a VPC, strict egress rules, and our infra team wants to avoid public endpoints.
[01:38] Ari: We covered Private deployment options in the docs — for sandboxing we can spin up a dedicated private sandbox, or use a hosted sandbox with a VPC peering connector. We'll share the network checklist.
[01:52] Rajiv: Perfect. Can you show the actual console flow? we want to see suggestions and the expected delta on latency and token costs.
[02:00] Samira: Absolutely, let me share my screen — I'm in the Optimize tab, selecting the "QProfile Playbook" view. First panel shows model candidates and expected token perf. Note: these are estimates based on our kernel selector and observed sequence length distribution.
[02:25] Samira: Here is a sample QProfile we recommend for short prompts — INT8|AggressiveCache|Batch=8 — we estimate 30–40% latency improvement over fp16 with a 3–8% quality drift on our standard eval. For FP8 the latency delta is smaller but quality drift is often <2% on average.
[02:46] Emily: When you say quality drift, what's the eval? we need it to reflect our summarization prompt, otherwise it's not reassuring.
[02:55] Samira: Totally — that's why the console lets you upload a custom prompt set. You can run an on-demand sensitivity sweep; we do a paired A/B with your prompts and show per-example diffs, BLEU-like or chosen metric. The sandbox run will use your 500 sample prompts to estimate fidelity impact.
[03:16] Rajiv: We're worried about corner cases — hallucinations or hallucination-like truncations. How do you guard for those in a rollout?
[03:24] Samira: The Speedline playbook recommends three gates: unit tests on a prompt set, a canary traffic slice with active monitoring (we compare logits/outputs and compute divergence), and an automatic rollback if a threshold of regressions is hit. There's also a KV cache sanity check — note transcription sometimes calls it KV cash — it's the same thing.
[03:47] Ben: Are we able to see token-level latency and cost breakdowns per token so we can map to our billing lines?
[03:54] Ari: Yup, Console shows token-level latency, model time, and cost estimate by profile. We'll export a spreadsheet with cost per million tokens at observed throughput.
[04:08] Lina Park: Could you speak to dedicated vs hosted for this kind of work? We're leaning enterprise and want guaranteed performance.
[04:15] Samira: For strict latency SLOs Dedicated is often better because you get reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput. Hosted can be cheaper to start and supports quick experiments. For the Speedline path we often start on hosted sandbox to run sensitivity sweeps and then move to Dedicated for production canaries.
[04:34] Rajiv: Any gotchas with quantizing instruction-tuned models? we use a mix of base+instruction tuned variants.
[04:42] Samira: Instruction tuning changes activation distributions slightly; the console will recommend per-variant profiles. Sometimes an INT8 profile is fine for base but the instruction-tuned variant needs FP8 or a looser INT8 calibration. We capture that in the QProfile suggestions.
[05:03] Emily: Can you explain the difference in practical terms between INT8 and FP8 — my team still confuses them.
[05:10] Samira: Sure — INT8 is integer quantization that's typically cheaper and gives bigger latency wins on certain kernels but can be more brittle on outlier activations. FP8 preserves some dynamic range and often keeps fidelity closer to FP16 while still improving memory footprint. In our tests INT8 gives up to ~2x speed on some hardware but quality regressions can be higher; FP8 is a middle ground.
[05:40] Rajiv: What about mixed precision per-layer? do you expose that or is it an internal kernel decision?
[05:46] Samira: We do layered heuristics but the console abstracts it — you pick a profile and our compilation and kernel selector decides per-layer paths. Advanced users can export the profile and we provide a tuning script.
[06:04] Ari: Quick aside — auditors ask about SOC2 and key management when we talk about private deployments. We have SOC2 Type 2, SSO via SAML/Okta, and KMS integrations including customer-managed keys. We'll attach the security pack.
[06:20] Rajiv: Good. Can you quantify rollback sensitivity? like if 5% of prompts diverge more than X, we roll back. How does that look in the console?
[06:31] Samira: In the canary panel you define thresholds: divergence percent, latency regressions, and a severity-weighted score. If the score exceeds the threshold we auto-fallback to the previous profile. You can tune thresholds per-route.
[06:47] Emily: We have a lot of short-form queries (avg 25 tokens) and occasional long documents. How does sequence length distribution affect the benefit of INT8/FP8?
[06:58] Samira: For short sequences the overhead dominates, so batching and kernel latency matter more — INT8 can still help but you'll get less relative win. For long sequences INT8/FP8 helps more on memory and KV cache footprint, giving both latency and throughput benefits. The console shows by-percentile expected gains based on your uploaded distribution.
[07:25] Ben: Any special monitoring we should add to our side to detect subtle quality degradation post-rollout?
[07:32] Samira: Yes, we recommend a signal mix: synthetics (your prompt set diff), production divergence sampling (we sample a percentage and compute similarity), and functional checks (key business correctness tests). We can wire up tracing hooks to your observability stack.
[07:51] Rajiv: Can we test hardware variance? we might run on A100s in prod but use different GPUs in Dedicated.
[07:58] Samira: Console lets you select hardware profile for the estimates; we also provide benchmark artifacts for specific instance types. If you want, Samira: I'll run a quick sample bench now with the public benchmarks and show relative numbers for A100 vs H100.
[08:12] Samira: Running a synthetic short prompt loop — rough numbers: FP16 baseline p95 92ms, FP8 p95 78ms (15% improvement), INT8 p95 55ms (40% improvement) on the H100 with batch=8. But note those are synthetic — real prompts can shift the numbers.
[08:40] Emily: That's encouraging. What's the recommended canary slice size to catch regressions quickly?
[08:45] Samira: 1–5% for low risk, 5–10% for reasonable sensitivity. We also do progressive ramping: 1% -> 5% -> 20% over a few hours with monitoring.
[08:58] Rajiv: Regarding billing, does switching to INT8 change token accounting? we bill tokens at the model layer currently.
[09:06] Ari: Token accounting remains, but cost per-token is reduced because compute per token drops; the console cost model shows expected $/million tokens for each profile. We'll run a custom estimate with your qps to provide a monthly spend projection.
[09:19] Lina Park: On governance — can we restrict who can flip profiles in a route? We need RBAC.
[09:26] Samira: RBAC is supported — you can restrict profile edits and rollout approvals to specific roles. Audit logs are retained and exportable.
[09:34] Rajiv: Any known model classes that fail with INT8 more frequently?
[09:38] Samira: Very large instructioned chat-style models with heavy system prompts can be sensitive, and some autoregressive sampler ops show more variance. We recommend FP8 or hybrid approaches for that class.
[09:55] Ben: What's the expected QA effort from our side for a full rollout?
[09:59] Samira: For our typical Speedline flow: upload prompt set (your 500 samples), run sensitivity sweep (1–2 days), review per-example diffs (2–3 engineers, 1 day), canary ramp (couple hours), then monitor for 72 hours. So roughly 3–5 engineering days of effort spread across teams.
[10:22] Rajiv: Can you provide sample automation for the canary rollback hooks? we use Terraform and have a CI pipeline.
[10:29] Samira: Yes, we have a Terraform provider example and a webhook-based rollback integration. We'll share the repo link.
[10:36] Emily: For the sandbox run, how isolated is data? we will send customer prompts maybe including PII—how is that handled?
[10:43] Ari: For sandbox runs we can enable private sandbox with data never leaving your VPC if you choose Private deployment. Hosted sandboxes redact or encrypt artifacts; we'll provide the data handling docs.
[10:55] Rajiv: Ok let's talk about the specific experiments we want: run FP8 and INT8 with our 500 prompts, show per-example diffs and a cost model. If FP8 gives <1% drift and 15% cost savings vs fp16, it's probably a safe win.
[11:12] Samira: Noted. Also want to flag that for certain prompts we might need per-prompt-profile tags — console supports tagging problem prompts so you can exclude them from certain profiles.
[11:24] Ben: We'll check our network team for peering. If we do a private sandbox, how long to spin that up?
[11:30] Ari: Usually 3–5 business days for private sandbox provisioning; hosted sandbox is immediate.
[11:36] Rajiv: Great. Anything else in the playbook we should be aware of?
[11:40] Samira: We also capture rollback runbooks and a decision matrix — aggressive vs conservative profiles with recommended monitoring thresholds. The Speedline playbook includes an SLA-aligned recommendation if you choose Dedicated.
[11:55] Lina: Can we embed our business metrics in the monitoring? like conversion lift or NPS?
[12:00] Samira: Yes, the observability hooks can accept custom signals so you can align model regressions with business KPIs.
[12:08] Ari: Ok let's recap next steps: we'll share the benchmark spreadsheet, security pack, terraform examples, and schedule a sandbox hands-on. Samira will run the FP8/INT8 stress test once Emily sends the prompt set.
[12:21] Rajiv: Sounds good. I'm particularly interested in the progressive ramp pattern and the failure thresholds. Also want to see the per-example diffs so our product team can review.
[12:31] Emily: We'll get the prompts over by Friday. Thanks for the walkthrough.
[12:36] Ben: Thanks everyone.
[12:38] Ari: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the links and schedule — talk soon.

End of transcript.
